# Don't re-read yourself {#sec-drry}

You have almost certainly written the same twenty lines of code three times, with one thing changed each time. I have done it more times than I would like to admit. This session is about why that hurts, and it is not the reason you have probably been told.

::: {.overview}

## Overview {.unnumbered}

**Duration** 60 minutes

**Questions**

<!-- These map onto the sections below, in order. If you move a section, move its question. -->

- Why is repeated code so hard to work with?
- What is DRRY, and how is it different from DRY?
- If repetition isn't the reason to write a function, what is?
- When should I *not* write a function?
- What do I actually get out of this?

**What you need this session**

- A session of RStudio open
- Something to draw on, and something to draw with

No packages this session. Everything here uses data that ships with R.

:::

## The problem functions solve

I do not think I can overstate this: learning to write functions changed how I think about code, and how I think about solving problems. It does take a while to develop, but the payoff is enormous.

A function is not only a way to avoid typing something twice. It's a way to take complexity and express it in a form you can reason with.

Once you can do that, you can hold a bigger problem in your head. It is like learning a word for a thing you already knew about:

> Benighted: Unexpectedly caught out in the dark

> Scrumping: To steal fruit such as apples from trees

My own journey into functions started in 2013. I was writing code to calculate a t-test from scratch. I had my reasons! At the top of the script was something like:

```r
var_1 <- data$x1
var_2 <- data$x2
```

and then a pile of code that computed the result.

::: {.callout-tip title="The whole script, if you want to see it" collapse="true"}

This is roughly what it looked like. What I would like you to notice is how much of it there is, and where the two lines I kept editing are.

```r
var_1 <- data$x1                                              # <1>
var_2 <- data$x2                                              # <1>

n_1 <- length(var_1)
n_2 <- length(var_2)

mean_1 <- mean(var_1)
mean_2 <- mean(var_2)

var_within_1 <- sum((var_1 - mean_1)^2) / (n_1 - 1)
var_within_2 <- sum((var_2 - mean_2)^2) / (n_2 - 1)

pooled_var <- ((n_1 - 1) * var_within_1 + (n_2 - 1) * var_within_2) / (n_1 + n_2 - 2)
std_error <- sqrt(pooled_var * (1 / n_1 + 1 / n_2))

t_statistic <- (mean_1 - mean_2) / std_error
degrees_freedom <- n_1 + n_2 - 2
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_statistic), df = degrees_freedom)

t_statistic
p_value
```

1. These two lines are the only part that ever changed.

:::

Every time I wanted to look at a different pair of variables, I went back to the top, changed those two lines, and ran the whole thing again.

Two lines out of twenty changed, and I re-ran all of them by hand, every single time.

![Four runs of the same script. Two bars change colour.](figs/two-lines-of-twenty.png){fig-alt="Four copies of the same script side by side, drawn as rows of grey bars rather than readable code. In every copy the top two rows are coloured, a different colour in each copy, and the remaining eighteen rows are identical grey. A label underneath reads: two lines changed, the other eighteen ran again anyway, every single time." width=100%}

Something about that felt wrong at the time. But I didn't have the words for it.

What I was reaching for sounded like this:

> I want to run this script, but get the top couple of lines to change depending on which variables I specify.

What I needed was a function, and I just did not have the words for it.

I had been **taught** functions by then, and I had been **using** functions the whole time, things like `lm()`, `table()`, `subset()` and `read.csv()`. I used them every day without once thinking about where they came from, or that I could make my own.

But the examples I was taught with were "convert Celsius to Fahrenheit" and "identify odd numbers", and I couldn't see how those applied to anything I actually did.

They seemed like useful kitchen trinkets. An apple corer, a garlic press. They did not look like a fundamental skill, the way knowing how to use a knife does.

Functions are the knife.

### A bug you can't see

Rather than argue that, let me show you. What does this code do?

We'll use `penguins`, which comes with R from version 4.5.0.

```{r}
#| label: penguins-head
head(penguins)
```

Now have a proper look at this.

```{r}
#| label: drry-centre-scale
bill_len <- penguins$bill_len
bill_dep <- penguins$bill_dep

bill_len_0 <- (bill_len - mean(bill_len, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(bill_len, na.rm = TRUE)
bill_dep_0 <- (bill_dep - mean(bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(bill_len, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Your Turn"}

::: {.callout-tip title="Setup code" collapse="true"}

```{r}
#| ref.label: ["drry-centre-scale"]
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```

:::

Here is the code again. Don't run it.

```r
bill_len_0 <- (bill_len - mean(bill_len, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(bill_len, na.rm = TRUE)
bill_dep_0 <- (bill_dep - mean(bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(bill_len, na.rm = TRUE)
```

1. In one sentence, what is this code doing?
2. There is a bug in it. Find it.
3. How long did that take, and what made it hard?

:::

So what is it doing?

This is mean centring and scaling. It gives your data a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, which some statistical models want.

Reading that code, it is hard to see that this is what is happening. Nothing in it says "centre and scale". You have to reconstruct the intent from the arithmetic.

And there **is** an error.

Look at the second line again. For `bill_dep_0` I divide by the standard deviation of **`bill_len`**, not `bill_dep`.

That is a copy-paste bug, it is completely silent, and it produces numbers that look entirely plausible:

```{r}
#| label: drry-plausible
head(bill_dep_0, 3)
```

Nothing about those numbers says "wrong". If you found it, well done, and if you did not, that is exactly why I would rather not rely on either of us spotting it.

There is a way to catch it, and it's worth noticing now because the whole course comes back to it. Scaling is supposed to give you a standard deviation of 1. So ask:

```{r}
#| label: drry-check
sd(bill_dep_0, na.rm = TRUE)
```

That should be 1, and it is not. The failure never raised an error, never printed a warning, and would have gone into a model perfectly happily. We only found it because we went and looked.

A function fixes this by taking away the need to write the variable in each time. Break it into two steps:

```{r}
#| label: drry-two-steps
mean_center <- function(variable) {
  variable - mean(variable, na.rm = TRUE)
}

scale_sd <- function(variable) {
  variable / sd(variable, na.rm = TRUE)
}
```

Now we can write:

```{r}
#| label: drry-piped
bill_len |>
  mean_center() |>
  scale_sd() |>
  head(3)
```

Or make one function that does both:

```{r}
#| label: drry-center-scale
center_scale <- function(variable) {
  centered <- mean_center(variable)
  centered_scaled <- scale_sd(centered)
  centered_scaled
}
```

Each function **says what it does** in its name. Reading `center_scale`, you can see it does a thing called `mean_center` first, and then a thing called `scale_sd`.

Compare the original:

```r
bill_len_0 <- (bill_len - mean(bill_len, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(bill_len, na.rm = TRUE)
bill_dep_0 <- (bill_dep - mean(bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(bill_len, na.rm = TRUE)
```

with:

```{r}
#| label: drry-fixed
bill_len_0 <- center_scale(bill_len)
bill_dep_0 <- center_scale(bill_dep)

sd(bill_dep_0, na.rm = TRUE)
```

You cannot even write the bug now, because there is nowhere left to put it.

::: {.callout-tip title="Someone has probably done this already" collapse="true"}

Base R has `scale()`, which centres and scales the columns of a numeric matrix. That's our two steps, in one call.

```{r}
#| label: drry-base-scale
head(center_scale(bill_len), 3)
head(scale(bill_len), 3)
```

Same numbers. `scale()` hands back a matrix, because it's built to do every column at once.

Which is a good argument for checking whether a solution exists before writing your own.

At worst you find nobody has solved your problem, which is an opportunity. Usually you learn the words other people use for it, and your next search goes much better.

:::

**What to hold onto here.** The bug survived because the code was hard to read, not because it was repeated. Twice is not many. It was still too many to read carefully.

## Don't re-read yourself

Here is the move this whole course turns on.

Repetition is one way to make code expensive. Re-reading is the cost underneath it.

Code can be written once, never repeated, and still charge you every single time you come back to it. Here is a line I have written versions of many times:

```{r}
#| label: drry-nested
round(
  sum(!is.na(airquality$Ozone) & airquality$Ozone > 30) /
    sum(!is.na(airquality$Ozone)) * 100,
  1
)
```

That appears exactly once, so DRY has nothing to say about it. And you still cannot read it.

You can only work it out by running it in your head, from the inside out. Count the days above 30. Count the days with a reading at all. Divide. Times a hundred. Round.

So it is fifty point nine percent of something. Of what, exactly?

Give the idea a name and the question goes away:

```{r}
#| label: drry-pct-above
pct_above <- function(x, threshold) {
  above <- sum(x > threshold, na.rm = TRUE)
  recorded <- sum(!is.na(x))
  round(above / recorded * 100, 1)
}

pct_above(airquality$Ozone, threshold = 30)
```

Same answer. But now the line tells you what it is for, and the two intermediate names tell you what the division means. Half the recorded ozone days were above 30.

You do not re-read the body, you read the name and carry on.

::: {.callout-note title="Your Turn"}

::: {.callout-tip title="Setup code" collapse="true"}

```{r}
#| ref.label: ["drry-pct-above"]
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```

:::

1. Say out loud what this does, before you run it or edit it. Time yourself.

    ```r
    round(mean(airquality$Temp[!is.na(airquality$Ozone)]) -
            mean(airquality$Temp[is.na(airquality$Ozone)]), 2)
    ```

2. Now write down, in one sentence, what it's **for**. That sentence is the name of a function.
3. Use `pct_above()` to find what percentage of days had a temperature above 80.

::: {.callout-tip title="Starting code" collapse="true"}

```r
pct_above(x = ___, threshold = ___)
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

Only open this if you have had a go.

```{r}
#| label: drry-answer
pct_above(airquality$Temp, threshold = 80)
```

The first one compares mean temperature on days where ozone was recorded against days where it was missing. A reasonable name would be `temp_gap_by_missingness()`, or something you'd rather read than that.

:::

:::

**What to hold onto here.** The trigger is not "have I typed this three times", it is "have I had to read this again to work out what it does".

## Don't repeat yourself, as the special case

You will often be told **DRY**: Don't Repeat Yourself. Copy and paste the same code three times, and you should write a function.

That is true, and I am not arguing with it. But it treats the symptom rather than the cause.

You only end up repeating yourself because you could not express the idea in the first place. If the idea had a name, you would have called it by name. So the cause is expression, and repetition is what it looks like from outside.

The version I prefer is **DRRY**: Don't Re-Read Yourself.^[Naming credit to [Miles McBain](https://milesmcbain.xyz/).]

DRRY fires earlier than DRY, and it fires more often. It fires on the *first* copy rather than the third, and it fires when there is no copy at all, like the line above.

Every case DRY catches, DRRY catches too. That is what makes it the more useful rule. DRY is a special case of it, and a good one, because repeated code is nearly always code you could not say plainly.

::: {.callout-caution title="Some history: where DRY comes from" collapse="true"}

DRY was named by Andrew Hunt and David Thomas in [The Pragmatic Programmer](https://pragprog.com/titles/tpp20/the-pragmatic-programmer-20th-anniversary-edition/), in 1999.

Their actual wording is worth reading, because it is not the version that gets repeated:

> Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system.

**Knowledge**, not code. They were never really talking about typing the same characters twice. The version that survived is the one that is easy to check, which is not the same as the one that is useful.

:::

## When not to write a function

If repetition isn't the trigger, you need to know what *is*. The fastest way to get there is to look at when the answer is no.

**When it's used once and already reads plainly.**

```r
adult_penguins <- penguins[penguins$body_mass > 4000, ]
```

There is nothing to abstract. Wrapping that in `filter_adults()` adds a name you have to learn, and hides a line you could already read. You now have two things instead of one.

**When you can't name it.**

If you can't say what the function is for in a short phrase, that is information. Usually it means the block is doing two things, and the honest fix is two functions, not one with a vague name.

`process_data()` and `run_analysis()` are what this looks like when you push through anyway. Both names describe the machine rather than the idea, and neither will help you in six weeks.

**When the abstraction hides more than it saves.**

A function that takes seven arguments, four of which change every call, is not managing complexity, it is relocating it. You still have to hold all seven in your head, and now you have to hold the function's name as well.

**When the repetition is a coincidence.**

Two blocks that look identical today, for unrelated reasons, will drift apart. Merging them means every future change has to ask "does this apply to both?" That is a cost you pay forever, in order to save one paste.

This is the case people get wrong most often, because it is the one that looks most like DRY.

::: {.callout-note title="Your Turn"}

For each of these, decide: function, or leave it?

1. A three line block that reads a CSV, renames one column and drops another. It appears in four scripts.
2. `mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)`, written in eleven places.
3. Forty lines that clean the 2023 data, and forty nearly identical lines that clean the 2024 data. The differences are the file path and one column name.
4. A line computing BMI from weight and height, once.

There are no marks for the answers. What I am after is the reason you give, because the reason is the skill.

:::

**What to hold onto here.** "Would I have to read this again to know what it does?" If no, leave it alone.

## What you get out of this

Three things, and they build on each other.

**Speed of thought.** When the ideas in your analysis have names, you can think in those names. You stop holding six lines of arithmetic in working memory and start holding one phrase. That is more room for the actual problem.

**Speed of work.** You stop re-running twenty lines to change two. You stop hunting for the line you need to edit. Small savings, several times an hour, every day.

**Trust.** This is the one I care most about.

In statistics we often cannot test our way to confidence. There is no known right answer to compare against, which is usually the whole reason we are doing the analysis.

So we're left with reasoning. Can I read this code and convince myself it does what I meant?

`center_scale()` is a better answer to that question than the two lines it replaced. Not because it is shorter, but because you can check it once and then trust it everywhere it appears. The version with the arithmetic inline has to be checked every single time, and we already know how that goes.

## Summary {.unnumbered}

1. **Re-reading is the cost.** Repetition is one way to pay it, and not the only one.
2. **DRRY fires before DRY.** On the first copy, and often when there's no copy at all.
3. **A function is an idea with a name on it.** If you cannot name it, you do not have an idea yet.
4. **Sometimes the answer is no.** Used once and readable, a coincidental match, or an abstraction that hides more than it saves.
5. **Silent failures are the ones to fear.** `sd()` should have been 1. Nothing told us that it was not.
